narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the 2nd decile is well below the average of roughly 5.8 among accepted students, signaling that your later academic performance was weaker than most who succeed. Your first-year ranking in the 3rd decile (versus an average of 6.0 for accepted applicants) added further weight in the same direction, though with less impact.

Your LSAT score of 35 worked in the opposite direction. While it is slightly below the accepted average of 37.2, it still provided a modest pull toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the academic ranking signals.

Your low family income, undergraduate GPA of 3.10, and full-time study plans also played smaller roles but were not decisive.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, aim for a higher LSAT score, and consider targeted bar-prep programs that address the specific weaknesses shown here. Reapply once you can demonstrate clearer evidence of readiness to pass the bar. (218 words)
